content: Every request starts with a request line: METHOD, path, and HTTP version, e.g. GET /users/42 HTTP/1.1.
Headers are key-value metadata lines that follow the request line; they describe the client, what it accepts, and how the body is encoded.
The status line carries the HTTP version, a three-digit status code, and a short reason phrase like 200 OK.
The status code is the machine-readable verdict; the reason phrase is decorative and clients should not depend on it.
GET retrieves a representation and must not change server state; it is both safe and idempotent.
POST submits data for processing; it is neither safe nor idempotent, so clients should not blindly retry it.
1xx is informational, 2xx means success, 3xx means go look elsewhere, 4xx means the client messed up, 5xx means the server did.
200 OK, 201 Created, and 204 No Content cover nearly all success cases; reach for 201 when you made something new.
Host identifies which virtual site the client wants; without it one server cannot serve many domains on one IP.
Content-Type declares the body's media type and charset, e.g. application/json; charset=utf-8; Content-Length gives its byte size.
The server sends Set-Cookie headers; the browser stores them in a cookie jar and returns matching ones on future requests.
Domain and Path scope where a cookie is sent; narrower scope means less exposure.
Freshness says a cached copy may be reused without asking: Cache-Control: max-age=3600 lets a cache serve it for an hour.
Validation says the cache must check first: ETag or Last-Modified let the server answer 304 Not Modified instead of resending the body.
The client advertises capabilities with Accept (media types), Accept-Language, Accept-Encoding, and Accept-Charset.
Quality values (q=0.9) rank preferences; the server chooses the highest-ranked type it can produce.
301 Moved Permanently and 308 Permanent Redirect are cacheable and signal a lasting move; use them for canonical URLs.
302 Found and 307 Temporary Redirect signal a short-term detour, such as post-login landing pages.
HTTP/1.0 opened a new TCP connection per request; HTTP/1.1 added persistent keep-alive connections and pipelining.
HTTP/1.1 suffers head-of-line blocking: one slow response stalls everything behind it on the same connection.
Resources are nouns: /orders, /orders/42, /orders/42/items. Verbs belong in HTTP methods, not in paths.
A collection (/orders) and its members (/orders/42) are different resources with different methods allowed.
POST that creates returns 201 with a Location header pointing at the new resource.
Successful PUT and PATCH return 200 with the updated representation, or 204 when there is nothing to return.
Offset pagination (?offset=40&limit=20) is simple but skips or duplicates rows when data changes between pages.
Page-number pagination has the same drift problem and gets slow on deep pages in most databases.
Filters are query parameters naming fields: ?status=shipped&region=west; keep the vocabulary tied to resource fields.
Sorting uses a sort parameter with - for descending: ?sort=-created_at; whitelist sortable fields.
Every error response shares one envelope: a stable machine code, a human message, and optional details.
Machine codes (ORDER_LIMIT_EXCEEDED) stay stable across versions; human messages may be reworded freely.
Path versioning (/v1/orders) is the most visible and the easiest to route, cache, and document.
Header or media-type versioning keeps URLs clean but is invisible in browser bars and harder to debug.
GET, PUT, DELETE, HEAD, and OPTIONS are idempotent by contract; repeating them must not change the outcome.
POST is not idempotent, which is exactly why payment and order endpoints need idempotency keys.
Limits are usually expressed per key or per IP per window: 1000 requests per hour, 10 per second burst.
Fixed windows are simple; sliding windows and token buckets smooth bursts more fairly.
A webhook is an HTTP POST your system sends when something happens; the receiver must answer 2xx quickly.
Sign every payload with HMAC so receivers can verify it came from you and was not tampered with.
OpenAPI describes paths, operations, parameters, request/response schemas, and security schemes in one document.
The spec is the contract: generate documentation, client SDKs, and mock servers from it instead of hand-writing each.
The doctype <!DOCTYPE html> triggers standards mode; without it browsers fall back to quirks mode with legacy layout bugs.
The head holds metadata invisible on the page: title, charset, viewport, stylesheets, and scripts.
Semantic elements describe role: <nav> is navigation, <article> is self-contained content, <aside> is tangential.
Screen readers offer landmark navigation built from these elements; divs give them nothing to work with.
Every input needs an associated <label>; placeholders are hints, not labels, and vanish when typing starts.
Input types (email, tel, number, date) summon the right mobile keyboard and free validation.
Tables are for tabular data, not layout; CSS handles layout now.
<thead>, <tbody>, and <tfoot> group rows so headers repeat and styling targets structure.
Images need alt text describing their purpose; decorative images get empty alt so they are skipped.
All interactive elements must be reachable and operable by keyboard, with a visible focus indicator.
charset and viewport are functional: they affect decoding and mobile layout directly.
The description meta often becomes the search-result snippet; write it like ad copy for the page.
An iframe embeds a full separate document with its own origin, scripts, and storage.
The sandbox attribute strips capabilities by default; allow-scripts and allow-same-origin re-grant them selectively.
Every element is a box: content at the center, then padding, border, and margin moving outward.
By default, width sets only the content box; padding and border add to the total size.
Specificity is scored per selector: ids outweigh classes, classes outweigh element names.
Inline styles beat all selectors; !important beats everything and should be reserved for utilities and overrides.
Inheritance passes some properties (color, font, line-height) from parent to child automatically.
Layout properties (margin, padding, border, width) do not inherit; each element starts fresh.
Flexbox lays out along one axis: the main axis (row or column) and the perpendicular cross axis.
justify-content aligns along the main axis; align-items aligns along the cross axis.
Grid lays out in two dimensions at once: define columns and rows on the container, place items into cells.
grid-template-columns: 1fr 2fr 1fr creates three tracks with the middle twice as wide; fr is a share of free space.
Fluid layouts use relative units (%, fr, vw) so content stretches instead of snapping at fixed widths.
Media queries apply styles conditionally: @media (min-width: 768px) targets viewports at least that wide.
Custom properties are declared with --name and read with var(--name, fallback).
They follow normal cascade and inheritance, so a subtree can override a token for everything inside it.
const is the default: it binds the name, though the object it points to can still change.
let allows reassignment and is block-scoped to the nearest { } pair.
A closure is a function bundled with the variables that were in scope when it was created.
Function declarations are hoisted whole; function expressions and arrows are not.
A promise represents a future value with three states: pending, fulfilled, rejected.
async/await lets you write async logic in straight-line style; await pauses only that function.
fetch returns a promise of a Response; it only rejects on network failure, not on HTTP error statuses.
Always check response.ok (or the status) before parsing; a 404 still resolves the promise.
querySelector and querySelectorAll find elements with CSS selectors; getElementById is the fastest single lookup.
textContent sets plain text safely; innerHTML parses HTML and must never receive untrusted strings.
addEventListener attaches handlers without clobbering others; one element can have many listeners.
Events bubble from the target up through ancestors; capture phase runs the other way down.
JSON.parse throws on malformed input; always parse inside try/catch at trust boundaries.
JSON.stringify drops functions, undefined, and symbols, and converts dates to ISO strings silently.
Each module has its own scope; nothing is global unless explicitly attached to window.
Named exports (export function) allow many per module; default export (export default) allows one.
localStorage persists across sessions on one origin (~5MB); sessionStorage dies with the tab.
Both store strings only; JSON.stringify on the way in, JSON.parse on the way out.
Name the columns you need; SELECT * is fine for exploration but wasteful and brittle in applications.
WHERE filters rows before any grouping or ordering; put the most selective conditions where indexes can use them.
INNER JOIN keeps only rows with a match on both sides; it is the default mental model for related data.
LEFT JOIN keeps every row from the left table, filling NULLs where the right side has no match.
Aggregates collapse rows: COUNT counts, SUM/AVG total and average numerics, MIN/MAX find extremes.
GROUP BY partitions rows first, then aggregates each group separately.
INSERT names its columns explicitly so schema changes do not silently shift values into wrong columns.
UPDATE and DELETE without WHERE affect every row; always write WHERE first, then the rest of the statement.
Every table gets a primary key; surrogate integer or UUID keys keep identity stable when business keys change.
Foreign keys declare relationships and, with the right actions, prevent or cascade orphaned rows.
An index is a separate data structure the planner can use to find rows without scanning the table.
B-tree indexes serve equality and range queries on the indexed columns' leading edge.
A transaction groups statements into one atomic unit: all commit together or all roll back.
ACID promises atomicity, consistency, isolation, and durability for committed work.
Parameters ($1, ?, :name) send values separately from the SQL text; the database never parses values as code.
String concatenation of user input into SQL is the vulnerability; parameterization is the fix.
First normal form: atomic values, one value per cell, no repeating groups.
Second normal form: every non-key column depends on the whole key, not part of a composite key.
A supervisor (systemd, runit, a container runtime) starts your process, watches it, and restarts it on failure.
Restart policies need backoff: immediate tight-loop restarts on a persistent crash burn CPU and fill logs.
A reverse proxy sits in front of app servers, accepting client connections and forwarding requests inward.
It terminates TLS, so app servers speak plain HTTP on a trusted network and certificates live in one place.
server blocks select by Host; location blocks inside them match paths with prefix or regex rules.
proxy_pass forwards to upstreams; pairing it with header forwarding keeps the app informed.
TLS encrypts traffic in transit, protecting against eavesdropping and tampering on the path.
The handshake negotiates a version and cipher, then the server proves identity with a certificate.
Automated CAs (like ACME-based issuers) make certificates free and renewable by software, not by calendar.
Renewal must be automated AND verified: a cron job that silently fails is the same as no cron job.
Structured logs (JSON with named fields) are queryable; free-text logs are archaeology.
Every request gets a trace id propagated through services so one user's journey is one query.
Liveness asks 'is it running'; readiness asks 'can it serve traffic right now'.
A service can be alive but not ready (warming caches, migrations running); only readiness should gate traffic.
Configuration lives in the environment, not in code: env vars or mounted config, never hard-coded.
Secrets are configuration with extra handling: injected from a vault or secret store, never in repos or images.
SIGTERM means 'please stop soon'; SIGKILL means 'stop now' with no cleanup.
On SIGTERM: stop accepting new work, finish in-flight requests, close connections, then exit.
Validate on the server; client-side checks are UX, not security, and attackers bypass them freely.
Prefer allowlists (known-good patterns) over denylists (known-bad signatures attackers mutate around).
XSS happens when attacker-controlled data is interpreted as code by the browser.
Encode output for its context: HTML-encode in HTML, JS-encode in scripts, URL-encode in URLs.
Parameterized queries separate code from data at the protocol level; injection becomes impossible by construction.
The vulnerability is string concatenation of input into SQL; the fix is never concatenating input into SQL.
CSRF exploits the browser's automatic cookie sending: a malicious page triggers a request your session authorizes.
Synchronizer tokens (per-session, per-form secrets) prove the request came from your rendered page.
Never reveal whether the username or password was wrong; 'invalid credentials' covers both.
Rate-limit and progressively delay login attempts; lockouts should be temporary and logged.
Store salted hashes, never plaintext or reversible encryption; the server should not know the password.
Use a password-hashing function built for the job (bcrypt, scrypt, Argon2), not a fast general hash.
Session ids must be long, random, and unguessable; never derive them from usernames or timestamps.
Store session data server-side keyed by the id; the cookie carries only the random identifier.
Content-Security-Policy controls which sources can load scripts, styles, and frames: the strongest header you set.
Strict-Transport-Security tells browsers to use HTTPS only, for you and your subdomains, for a long max-age.
Every dependency is code you ship but did not write; its vulnerabilities become yours.
Pin versions with lockfiles so builds are reproducible and surprise upgrades cannot sneak in.
Disable TLS 1.0 and 1.1 and weak ciphers; support 1.2 with strong ciphers and prefer 1.3.
HSTS with includeSubDomains and a long max-age stops protocol-downgrade tricks.
HTTP 200 means the request succeeded; the response body carries the result.
HTTP 201 Created is returned when a POST successfully creates a new resource, usually with a Location header.
HTTP 204 No Content signals success with deliberately no response body.
HTTP 301 and 308 are permanent redirects; 302 and 307 are temporary.
HTTP 307 and 308 preserve the request method across the redirect; 301 and 302 historically may rewrite POST to GET.
HTTP 400 means the client sent malformed or invalid data.
HTTP 401 means missing or invalid credentials; 403 means authenticated but not permitted.
HTTP 404 means the requested resource does not exist on the server.
HTTP 409 Conflict signals a state clash such as a duplicate unique value or version mismatch.
HTTP 422 Unprocessable Entity means the request was well-formed but semantically invalid.
HTTP 429 Too Many Requests tells the client it exceeded its rate limit; pair it with Retry-After.
HTTP 500 means an unexpected server-side failure; 503 means temporarily unable to serve.
GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, and TRACE are safe methods: they must not change server state.
GET, PUT, DELETE, HEAD, and OPTIONS are idempotent: repeating them has the same effect as once.
POST is neither safe nor idempotent, so clients must not blindly retry it without idempotency keys.
The Content-Type header declares the media type of the message body, e.g. application/json.
The Authorization header carries credentials, typically as a Bearer token; its value must never be logged.
The Location header gives the URL for redirects and newly created resources.
ETag and Last-Modified enable conditional requests; a 304 Not Modified answer means the cached copy is fresh.
Cache-Control: no-store forbids caching; no-cache allows storage but requires revalidation.
The Vary header tells caches which request headers affect the response variant.
Set-Cookie HttpOnly blocks JavaScript access to the cookie; Secure requires HTTPS; SameSite limits cross-site sending.
HTTP/2 multiplexes many streams over one TCP connection and compresses headers with HPACK.
HTTP/3 runs over QUIC on UDP so packet loss stalls only the affected stream, not the whole connection.
REST models APIs as nouns: collections like /orders and members like /orders/42.
Cursor pagination stays correct when data changes between pages; offset pagination can skip or duplicate rows.
An idempotency key lets clients safely retry POST requests without creating duplicates.
Webhooks should be HMAC-signed so receivers can verify authenticity and integrity.
OpenAPI documents paths, operations, schemas, and security in one machine-readable contract.
The HTML doctype <!DOCTYPE html> triggers standards mode in browsers.
The charset meta tag should be the first element in head so the browser decodes bytes correctly.
Every form input needs an associated label; placeholders are not labels.
Use button for actions and a for navigation; the choice determines keyboard behavior and semantics.
The sandbox attribute on iframes strips capabilities unless selectively re-granted.
box-sizing: border-box makes width include padding and border.
In the cascade, origin beats importance, importance beats specificity, specificity beats source order.
Flexbox is for one-dimensional layout; grid is for two-dimensional layout.
justify-content aligns along the flex main axis; align-items aligns along the cross axis.
CSS custom properties inherit, which is what makes token-based theming work.
const is the default declaration in modern JavaScript; let is for reassigned bindings; var is legacy.
A closure is a function bundled with the variables in scope where it was created.
fetch only rejects on network failure; HTTP error statuses must be detected via response.ok.
textContent sets plain text safely; innerHTML parses HTML and must never receive untrusted strings.
localStorage persists per origin and stores strings only; never put secrets or tokens in it.
JSON.parse throws on malformed input and must be wrapped in try/catch at trust boundaries.
In SQL, NULL never equals anything, not even NULL; use IS NULL and IS NOT NULL.
INNER JOIN keeps only matched rows; LEFT JOIN keeps all left rows with NULLs for missing matches.
WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after aggregation.
Bound parameters separate SQL code from data and make injection structurally impossible.
A transaction makes multi-statement changes atomic: all commit together or all roll back.
Composite index column order matters: equality-filtered columns go before range-filtered ones.
Third normal form means every non-key column depends only on the key, eliminating update anomalies.
A reverse proxy terminates TLS, routes by host or path, and buffers slow clients away from app workers.
Never trust X-Forwarded-For from arbitrary clients; only the proxy's forwarded headers are trustworthy.
Liveness asks if the process runs; readiness asks if it can serve traffic; only readiness should gate traffic.
Configuration belongs in the environment, not in code; secrets come from a vault, never from git.
On SIGTERM a service should stop accepting new work, drain in-flight requests, then exit.
Validate all input server-side; client-side validation is user experience, not security.
Prefer allowlists over denylists when validating input.
Keep template auto-escaping on; every raw/safe bypass on user data is an XSS risk.
Content Security Policy restricts where scripts may load from, containing injection damage.
Store passwords as Argon2/bcrypt/scrypt hashes with unique salts, never plaintext or fast hashes.
Session ids must be 128-bit cryptographic random, rotated at login, and expired by idle and absolute timeouts.
Anti-CSRF tokens prove state-changing requests came from your own pages.
HSTS tells browsers to use HTTPS only, defeating protocol-downgrade attacks.
Disable TLS 1.0 and 1.1; prefer TLS 1.3 with forward-secret ciphers.
Pin dependency versions with lockfiles and fail CI on known-critical vulnerabilities.
